warmup.q: A settlement reader emits three ids instantly, and the collector needs 30 ms to post each one. You add .flowOn(io) before collect. What is the order of the read and posted lines now?
options: read 1, posted 1, read 2, posted 2, read 3, posted 3, the same as without flowOn
read 1, read 2, read 3, then posted 1, posted 2, posted 3
posted 1, posted 2, posted 3, then the reads
The flow throws "Flow invariant is violated"
warmup.why: With a different dispatcher, flowOn runs the reader in a second coroutine and puts a 64-slot channel between the two sides. The reader's emit now only drops the id into the channel, so it reads all three lines before the first 30 ms posting is done. The invariant error is for withContext around emit, not for flowOn.

sections.h: Add flowOn and the print order changes
sections.html:
Take lesson 1's settlement reader and its ledger writer, and add one line: .flowOn(io), where io is a dispatcher with one thread named io-thread. The ledger write takes 30 ms. Predict the order of the six lines.

Java
// Java equivalent: a reader thread puts lines into a 64-slot BlockingQueue,
// and the main thread takes them out and posts them
BlockingQueue<String> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
new Thread(() -> { for (String id : ids) put(mailbox, id); put(mailbox, END); }, "io-thread").start();
for (String id = mailbox.take(); !id.equals(END); id = mailbox.take()) {
    Thread.sleep(30);                // the ledger write
    System.out.println("posted  " + id + "   on " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
}
Kotlin
settlementIds()                      // prints "read <id> on <thread>", then emits the id
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect { id ->
        delay(30)                    // the ledger write
        println("posted  $id   on ${Thread.currentThread().name}")
    }

Without flowOn you get lesson 1's pattern: read, posted, read, posted, all on main. With it:

read    pay-1   on io-thread
read    pay-2   on io-thread
read    pay-3   on io-thread
posted  pay-1   on main
posted  pay-2   on main
posted  pay-3   on main

The reader ran ahead. It read all three lines before the first posting finished, so its emit calls returned without waiting for the ledger. In lesson 1, emit couldn't return before the collector did. Something now sits between the two sides and holds values, and the two sides run on different threads. The Java twin prints the same six lines, and it shows what that something is: a queue.

Why not just wrap the read and the emit in withContext(io)? Lesson 2 showed what flow { } says to that: "Flow invariant is violated". It also showed why. A hand-written raw Flow without the check ran its collector on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1. The collector runs inside emit, so an emit on an IO thread drags the collector onto that thread too. If your ledger client isn't thread-safe, or holds a connection checked out for this request, that's a real bug. To move the reader and leave the collector alone, you have to break the call chain between them. That takes a second coroutine and a place to keep values in between.

Each line is read instantly; it prints which thread read it. */ fun settlementIds(): Flow<String> = flow { for (line in lines) { val id = line.substringBefore(",") println("read $id on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") emit(id) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() println("=== plain, as in lesson 1") settlementIds().collect { id -> delay(30) // the ledger write println("posted $id on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } println("=== with .flowOn(io)") settlementIds().flowOn(io).collect { id -> delay(30) println("posted $id on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } io.close() }

alt.title: FlowOnOrderJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnOrder.kt with flowOn: a reader thread puts lines into a BlockingQueue // with 64 slots, and the main thread takes them out and posts them. That queue is the channel // that flowOn builds. package workbench.flows.l03; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; public class FlowOnOrderJava { static final String END = "<end>"; // a queue can't be closed, so the reader sends an end marker public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { List<String> lines = List.of("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,990,EUR", "pay-3,12000,GBP"); BlockingQueue<String> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); Thread reader = new Thread(() -> { try { for (String line : lines) { String id = line.substring(0, line.indexOf(',')); System.out.println("read " + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); mailbox.put(id); // blocks only when all 64 slots are full } mailbox.put(END); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "io-thread"); reader.start(); for (String id = mailbox.take(); !id.equals(END); id = mailbox.take()) { Thread.sleep(30); // the ledger write System.out.println("posted " + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); } reader.join(); } }

try.expect: Without flowOn, read and posted alternate on main. With it, the three reads come first on io-thread, then the three postings on main. With flowOn(CoroutineName("reader")) the order goes back to read, posted, read, posted, all on main: the dispatcher didn't change, so there is no second coroutine and no channel. Section 3 comes back to this. The Java twin with a BlockingQueue prints the same six lines as the Kotlin version with 30 ms.

sections.h: What flowOn builds: a wall with a mailbox slot
sections.html:
You can build flowOn yourself from two coroutine tools you met in lesson 9 of the coroutines track: produce and a channel.

Java
// Java equivalent: an executor for the upstream and a 64-slot queue in between
static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream)
        throws InterruptedException {
    BlockingQueue<Object> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
    executor.execute(() -> {
        upstream.accept(value -> put(mailbox, value));   // the upstream's emit now means put
        put(mailbox, END);
    });
    for (Object v = mailbox.take(); v != END; v = mailbox.take()) downstream.accept((T) v);
}
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)                     // produce is experimental in 1.11.0
fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow {
    coroutineScope {
        val mailbox = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) {    // the second cook, behind the wall
            this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) }                 // the upstream's emit now means send
        }
        for (value in mailbox) emit(value)                     // we stay in the collector's coroutine
    }
}

Read it as a picture: a wall across the kitchen with a mailbox slot in it. Behind the wall, a second cook (the produce coroutine) runs on io and drops each plate into the mailbox. In front, the original diner takes plates out. Your emit calls now happen in the collector's own coroutine, so the inspector from lesson 2 has nothing to complain about. Nothing ever pushes a plate through the wall by hand.

The real flowOn does the same, with one shortcut. flowOn(ctx) returns a ChannelFlowOperatorImpl. When it is collected, it compares contexts. If the dispatcher is the same as the collector's, it runs the upstream inline with the new context and builds no channel. If the dispatcher differs, it runs coroutineScope { collector.emitAll(produceImpl(this)) }. That produce collects the upstream into a SendingCollector, whose emit is channel.send(value). The channel's default capacity is Channel.BUFFERED, which is 64.

Two measurements show it. First, a probe that holds the first value in the collector and counts how many emit calls return meanwhile. A plain flow gives 0. Both myFlowOn(io) and flowOn(io) give 65: 64 in the mailbox and one in the diner's hands. Then the 66th send suspends, because the mailbox is full. So flowOn doesn't remove backpressure. It moves it from "wait for the collector" to "wait for a free slot", and a slow ledger still slows the reader down, 64 lines later. Second, the collector's stack after flowOn(io):

    at HandMadeFlowOnKt$main$1$9.emit                                     <- your collector
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowKt__ChannelsKt.emitAllImpl$FlowKt__ChannelsKt   <- the drain loop
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowKt__ChannelsKt$emitAllImpl$1.invokeSuspend
    at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith

Your flow { } block is gone from it. It runs on another thread, in another coroutine, and only the drain loop, emitAllImpl, calls your collector.

code.title: HandMadeFlowOn.kt
code.html: @file:OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** flowOn by hand: a second coroutine on [dispatcher] sends into a 64-slot channel, and we drain it. */ fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val mailbox = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { // the second cook, behind the wall this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } // the upstream emits into the mailbox } for (value in mailbox) emit(value) // we stay in the collector's coroutine } } /** How many emits return while the collector still holds the first value? */ suspend fun ahead(label: String, op: (Flow<Int>) -> Flow<Int>) = coroutineScope { val returned = AtomicInteger() val gate = CompletableDeferred<Unit>() var received = 0 val source = flow { for (i in 1..200) { emit(i); returned.set(i) } } val job = launch { op(source).collect { received++; if (received == 1) gate.await() } } delay(200) // let the producer run as far as it can val heldAt = returned.get() gate.complete(Unit) job.join() println("%-22s emits returned while the collector held item 1: %3d (received %d)".format(label, heldAt, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() println("=== who runs where") flow { emit("pay-1"); println("emit pay-1 returned on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } .myFlowOn(io) .collect { println("myFlowOn: collected $it on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } flow { emit("pay-1"); println("emit pay-1 returned on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } .flowOn(io) .collect { println("flowOn: collected $it on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } println("=== how far ahead the producer gets") ahead("plain") { it } ahead("myFlowOn(io)") { it.myFlowOn(io) } ahead("flowOn(io)") { it.flowOn(io) } println("=== the collector's stack after flowOn(io)") flow { emit("pay-1") }.flowOn(io).collect { Thread.currentThread().stackTrace.drop(1) .takeWhile { !it.className.startsWith("kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask") } .forEach { println(" at ${it.className.removePrefix("workbench.flows.l03.")}.${it.methodName}") } } io.close() }

alt.title: HandMadeFlowOnJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of HandMadeFlowOn.kt: "flowOn" by hand with an executor and a 64-slot // BlockingQueue. The upstream runs on the executor; the consumer drains the queue on its own thread, // so the consumer's stack holds the draining loop and none of the reader's frames. package workbench.flows.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class HandMadeFlowOnJava { private static final Object END = new Object(); /** Runs upstream on executor, pushes its values through a queue, and delivers them on the caller's thread. */ @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> { try { mailbox.put(value); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); try { mailbox.put(END); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); for (Object v = mailbox.take(); v != END; v = mailbox.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); // the drain loop } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ExecutorService io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "io-thread")); Consumer<Consumer<String>> reader = emit -> { emit.accept("pay-1"); System.out.println("emit pay-1 returned on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); }; flowOn(io, reader, id -> { System.out.println("collected " + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); for (StackTraceElement f : Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()) System.out.println(" at " + f.getClassName().replace("workbench.flows.l03.", "") + "." + f.getMethodName()); }); io.shutdown(); } }

try.expect: The plain flow gives 0, and both myFlowOn(io) and flowOn(io) give 65: 64 in the channel plus the one the collector holds. Every version still receives all 200. The stack shows your collector called from emitAllImpl, and the flow block is not on it. With capacity = 10 your version gives 11. The Java consumer's stack has the drain loop (flowOn) and main, and none of the reader's frames.

sections.h: Several flowOn calls: rooms and walls
sections.html:
flowOn changes the context of the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn, and nothing below it. With two of them you get two walls and three rooms:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, publishOn moves what follows,
// and toStream() hands values back to the calling thread through a queue
Flux.range(1, 2)
    .doOnNext(i -> log("emit", i))
    .map(i -> { log("map1", i); return i; })
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .publishOn(cpu)
    .map(i -> { log("map2", i); return i; })
    .toStream()
    .forEach(i -> log("collect", i));
Kotlin
flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } }
    .map { log("map1", it); it }
    .flowOn(io)                                // wall 1: everything above runs on io
    .map { log("map2", it); it }
    .flowOn(cpu)                               // wall 2: map2 runs on cpu
    .collect { log("collect", it) }            // the collector's room: main

With coroutine debug mode on, the thread names count the coroutines for you:

  emit     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  emit     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map2     1   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  1   thread=main @coroutine#1
  map2     2   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  2   thread=main @coroutine#1

Three coroutines, so two channels. The order of lines across threads can change from run to run, but each stage always stays in its room. Notice the direction. Reactor's publishOn moves what comes after it. Kotlin's flowOn moves what comes before it. If you think in Reactor, read flowOn from the bottom up.

Three variants are worth knowing, because they surprise people. Two flowOn calls with nothing between them fuse into one wall, and the first one, nearest the source, wins: The toString() of flowOf(1, 2, 3).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) ends with ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]. (That string is a debug aid, not an API.) A map between them stops the fusion. Next, flowOn(CoroutineName("renamed")) keeps the dispatcher, so it builds no wall. The lines interleave on main like a plain flow, and the upstream's lines show main @renamed#1: the collector's coroutine number with a new name on it. Last, a Job in flowOn is refused as soon as you build the operator, with "Flow context cannot contain job in it."

flowOn never moves the collector. If the collecting side blocks, wrap the terminal call in withContext(io) { flow.collect { ... } }, as lesson 7 of the coroutines track showed.

code.title: FlowOnThreads.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors fun log(stage: String, v: Any?) = println(" %-8s %-3s thread=%s".format(stage, v, Thread.currentThread().name)) fun main() { // debug mode adds " @coroutine#N" to thread names, so you can count the coroutines System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on") val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() val cpu = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "cpu-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() runBlocking { println("=== two flowOn calls: two walls, three rooms") flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } } .map { log("map1", it); it } .flowOn(io) .map { log("map2", it); it } .flowOn(cpu) .collect { log("collect", it) } println("=== flowOn(CoroutineName): same dispatcher, so no wall") flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } } .flowOn(CoroutineName("renamed")) .collect { log("collect", it) } } println("=== adjacent flowOn calls fuse; toString() is a peek under the hood, not an API") val fused = flowOf(1, 2, 3).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) println(" " + fused.toString().substringAfter(" -> ")) println("=== a Job in flowOn is refused when the operator is built") try { flowOf(1).flowOn(Job()) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println(" " + e.message!!.substringBefore("Had")) } io.close(); cpu.close() }

alt.title: FlowOnThreadsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnThreads.kt with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source (the room behind // the first wall), publishOn moves what follows it (the second wall), and toStream() hands the // values back to the calling thread through a queue (the third room). Reactor moves downstream // with publishOn; Flow's flowOn moves upstream. package workbench.flows.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Scheduler; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnThreadsJava { static void log(String stage, Object v) { System.out.printf(" %-8s %-3s thread=%s%n", stage, v, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { Scheduler io = Schedulers.newSingle("io-thread"); Scheduler cpu = Schedulers.newSingle("cpu-thread"); Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext(i -> log("emit", i)) .map(i -> { log("map1", i); return i; }) .subscribeOn(io) .publishOn(cpu) .map(i -> { log("map2", i); return i; }) .toStream() .forEach(i -> log("collect", i)); io.dispose(); cpu.dispose(); } }

try.expect: emit and map1 run on io-thread @coroutine#3, map2 on cpu-thread @coroutine#2 and collect on main @coroutine#1: three coroutines and two channels. The fused flow prints ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]. With CoroutineName, emit and collect alternate on main, and the upstream shows @renamed#1. After the swap, emit and map1 run on cpu-thread and map2 on io-thread. The Reactor version puts emit and map1 on io-thread, map2 on cpu-thread and collect on main, using publishOn for the second wall.

sections.html:
Now fan in two acquirer feeds, north and east, into one flow. The obvious code is flow { } with a child coroutine per feed:

Java
// Java equivalent: two threads calling one consumer. Nothing stops them calling it at the same time.
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> north.forEach(collector::accept));
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> east.forEach(collector::accept));
Kotlin
flow {
    coroutineScope {
        launch { north.collect { emit(it) } }
        launch { east.collect { emit(it) } }
    }
}

It fails on the first value with an exact, helpful message:

Flow invariant is violated:
		Emission from another coroutine is detected.
		Child of StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@5a8e6209, expected child of BlockingCoroutine{Active}@4b4523f8.
		FlowCollector is not thread-safe and concurrent emissions are prohibited.
		To mitigate this restriction please use 'channelFlow' builder instead of 'flow'

This is the second half of the context check from lesson 2. Two launched children could call emit at the same moment, and the collector would run twice at once. So the inspector refuses any emit from a launched child.

channelFlow { } is the builder for this. It is a channel flow like the one flowOn builds, with a 64-slot mailbox (Channel.BUFFERED). Its block runs with a ProducerScope, which is both a CoroutineScope you can launch in and a SendChannel you can send to. Its KDoc says the scope "can be used concurrently from different contexts". Several cooks, one mailbox:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create gives a sink that several threads may call; you complete it yourself
Flux<Auth> both = Flux.create(sink -> {
    Thread n = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> north.forEach(sink::next));
    Thread e = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> east.forEach(sink::next));
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { join(n); join(e); sink.complete(); });
});
Kotlin
fun bothAcquirers(north: Flow<Auth>, east: Flow<Auth>): Flow<Auth> = channelFlow {
    launch { north.collect { send(it) } }
    launch { east.collect { send(it) } }
}

In a run with real threads, the builder block returned at t=17 ms, the four sends arrived from DefaultDispatcher-worker-1, every collect line printed on main, and the flow completed only at t=113 ms, after both children. The block may return early, and the flow still waits for every child. That is structured concurrency at work: the children belong to the producer coroutine's scope, and its channel closes only when that scope is done, so the collector's loop ends after the last send.

produceIn(scope) is the mailbox without the flow around it. It launches a coroutine in your scope that collects the flow, and returns the ReceiveChannel at once. The collecting starts at the caller's next suspension, whether or not anyone receives. It is hot: in the demo the upstream started and emitted 1 before anyone called receive. Consume it fully or cancel() it, because the scope waits for that producer coroutine like any other child.

try.title: Fan in two feeds
steps: Run ChannelFlowDemo.kt. Read the error from the flow { } version first.
In the channelFlow part, check three things: the thread of the sent lines, the thread of the collect lines, and when the flow completes compared with the builder block.
In the produceIn part, delete mailbox.cancel(). Predict what happens, then run it and stop it with Ctrl+C if it hangs.
Run ChannelFlowDemoJava.

code.title: ChannelFlowDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.channelFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.produceIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking var t0 = 0L fun at(s: String) = println(" t=%3d %-46s thread=%s".format(System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, s, Thread.currentThread().name)) fun main() = runBlocking { println("=== flow { } with two launched producers") try { flow { coroutineScope { launch { emit("north-1") } launch { emit("east-1") } } }.collect { println(" got $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println(" " + e.message!!.lines().drop(1).joinToString("\n ").trim()) } println("=== channelFlow: two acquirer feeds, one mailbox") t0 = System.currentTimeMillis() channelFlow { launch(Dispatchers.IO) { repeat(2) { delay(30); send("north-$it"); at("sent north-$it") } } launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(2) { delay(45); send("east-$it"); at("sent east-$it") } } at("builder block returns (children still running)") }.collect { at("collect $it") } at("channelFlow completed after both children") println("=== produceIn: a hot channel in your scope") t0 = System.currentTimeMillis() coroutineScope { val mailbox = flow { at("upstream started"); for (i in 1..4) { emit(i); at("emitted $i") } } .buffer(1) .produceIn(this) at("produceIn returned a ReceiveChannel") delay(100) at("receiving now: ${mailbox.receive()}") mailbox.cancel() at("cancelled the channel") } }

alt.title: ChannelFlowDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ChannelFlowDemo.kt: Reactor's Flux.create gives a sink that several threads may // call (it serializes them), much like channelFlow's send. We complete it only after both producer // threads are done, which channelFlow does for you. One difference shows in the output: there is no // mailbox here, so the subscriber runs on whichever producer thread calls next. package workbench.flows.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class ChannelFlowDemoJava { static long t0; static void at(String s) { System.out.printf(" t=%3d %-46s thread=%s%n", System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, s, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { t0 = System.currentTimeMillis(); Flux<String> both = Flux.create(sink -> { Thread north = Thread.ofVirtual().name("north-feed").start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { sleep(30); sink.next("north-" + i); at("sent north-" + i); } }); Thread east = Thread.ofVirtual().name("east-feed").start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { sleep(45); sink.next("east-" + i); at("sent east-" + i); } }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { north.join(); east.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } sink.complete(); // channelFlow completes after its children by itself }); at("create block returns (producers still running)"); }); both.doOnNext(v -> at("collect " + v)).blockLast(); at("flux completed after both producers"); } }

try.expect: The flow { } version fails with "Emission from another coroutine is detected" and the hint to use channelFlow. In the channelFlow part the sends come from a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, every collect line is on main, and the flow completes only after both children, well after the builder block returned. produceIn emits 1 before anyone receives. Without cancel() the program never ends: the producer waits forever on a full one-slot buffer, and the scope waits for it. The Java twin's subscriber runs on the producer threads, because a Reactor sink has no mailbox.

analogy: Picture the kitchen from lesson 1 with a wall built across it. flowOn(io) hires a second cook for the room behind the wall, on the IO shift, and sets a mailbox with 64 slots into the wall. The second cook drops plates into the mailbox and goes straight back to cooking; the diner in front takes them out one at a time. Two flowOn calls build two walls and three rooms. Two flowOn calls side by side build one wall, labelled with the first sign that was hung. flowOn(CoroutineName(...)) only repaints the sign on the same room, so there is no wall and no mailbox. channelFlow is several cooks in different rooms sharing one mailbox. And withContext around emit is a cook trying to push a plate through the wall by hand, which sets off the alarm. The picture breaks at the mailbox. A real mailbox is passive, but this one has a lock and a waiting line: when all 64 slots are full, the cook behind the wall is suspended until the diner takes one out, and when the diner stops collecting, the whole back room is cancelled.
world: Plenty of acquirer SDKs are still blocking: a reader for a settlement file on SFTP, a SOAP client, a JDBC call. In a Quarkus service, put flowOn(io) right under the blocking part, and keep the posting to the Oracle ledger in the collector. The ledger client is often tied to the caller, through a connection checked out from a pool of 20 for this job or a client that isn't thread-safe, and the collector is the only side that never moves. Fan-in is the other common case. When two acquirers report authorizations on separate feeds, channelFlow with one child per feed gives the risk engine a single stream. Remember that the children share one scope. If the north feed throws, the east feed is cancelled too and the whole flow fails, which is right for a reconciliation job and wrong for a live dashboard that should keep showing east.
mistake:
The most common mistake, especially for people who know Reactor, is putting flowOn at the end of a chain and expecting it to apply to everything, or to what comes after it. It applies only to the operators above it. Here the ledger postings, which must stay in the caller's context, end up on io too:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, and with no publishOn the postings run on io too
readLines(reader)
    .map(Settlement::parse)
    .doOnNext(ledger::post)          // runs on the io scheduler too
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .blockLast();
Kotlin
readLines(reader)
    .map { parseSettlement(it) }
    .onEach { ledger.post(it) }     // above flowOn, so this runs on io as well
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect()

People do it because Reactor's publishOn works on what follows it, and because "put the threading at the end" looks tidy. Read flowOn from the bottom up instead, and put it directly below the last line that must move: .map { parseSettlement(it) }.flowOn(io).onEach { ledger.post(it) }.

compare.title: flowOn by hand: a channel in Kotlin, a BlockingQueue in Java

java.title: HandMadeFlowOnJava.java (abridged)
java.html: // Java equivalent: an executor runs the upstream, a 64-slot queue sits in between static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> put(mailbox, value)); // blocks a thread when full put(mailbox, END); // a queue can't be closed: send a marker }); for (Object v = mailbox.take(); v != END; v = mailbox.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); }

kotlin.title: HandMadeFlowOn.kt (abridged)
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val mailbox = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } // suspends when full } // closes the channel when the block ends for (value in mailbox) emit(value) } }

compare.note: The shape is the same: a second worker, a 64-slot buffer, and a drain loop on the caller's side. Three things differ, and all of them matter in production. A full BlockingQueue blocks a thread, while a full channel suspends a coroutine. A queue can't be closed, so the Java version needs an end marker, while produce closes its channel when its block ends. And the Kotlin version stops cleanly: if the collector fails or stops early, coroutineScope cancels the produce coroutine. In the Java version the reader thread keeps running, blocked on a full queue, until someone interrupts it.

worked.title: Make the settlement import testable in virtual time

steps.say: The acquirer's file server allows one line per second, so the reader waits before each read. The first version hard-codes the dispatcher. A test with runTest looks fine but is slow, and its clock says nothing happened. In a run with three lines, TestTime.kt printed virtual=0 ms, wall=3180 ms: Dispatchers.Default lives outside the test scheduler, so its delay calls are real.
steps.code: fun slowFeed() = flow { repeat(3) { delay(1_000); emit(it) } } // one line per second runTest { slowFeed().flowOn(Dispatchers.Default).toList() // virtual=0 ms, wall=3180 ms }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: a hard-coded executor makes the test wait in real time too ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); List<Integer> lines = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> readThreeLinesSlowly(), io).join(); // 3 s of real waiting

steps.say: Inject the dispatcher instead. Production passes Dispatchers.IO, a test passes something else. Give it a default so callers don't have to care.
steps.code: fun importSettlements( reader: LineReader, ledger: Ledger, io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, // 1. injected, with the production default ): Flow<Settlement> = flow { while (true) emit(reader.readLine() ?: break) } .map { parseSettlement(it) } .flowOn(io) // 2. the wall uses whatever was passed in .onEach { ledger.post(it) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: take the Executor as a constructor argument final class SettlementImport { private final Executor io; // 1. injected SettlementImport(Executor io) { this.io = io; } CompletableFuture<List<Settlement>> readAll(LineReader reader) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> parseAll(reader), io); // 2. used here } }

steps.say: For timing tests, pass a test dispatcher that shares the test's scheduler. Its delay calls move the virtual clock, so the same three lines run in milliseconds and the clock reads exactly 3000. flowOn still builds its channel, because a second StandardTestDispatcher is a different dispatcher object.
steps.code: runTest { slowFeed().flowOn(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)).toList() // virtual=3000 ms, wall=8 ms }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: a direct executor runs the task on the test thread, with no real pool Executor direct = Runnable::run; List<Settlement> all = new SettlementImport(direct).readAll(fakeReader).join();

steps.say: For "which side ran where" tests, pass a real executor with one named thread, and record thread names in the fakes. That is how the lab's test checks that readLine ran on test-io and ledger.post on the test thread. Strip the @coroutine#N suffix that debug mode adds when tests run with -ea.
steps.code: val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "test-io") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() fun threadName() = Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @") val reader = LineReader { readOn += threadName(); lines.removeFirstOrNull() } val ledger = Ledger { postedOn += threadName() } // after collecting: readOn contains only "test-io", postedOn only the test thread

alt.html: ExecutorService io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "test-io")); LineReader reader = () -> { readOn.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); return lines.poll(); }; // after the run: readOn contains only "test-io"

lab.title: Move only the reader, then fan in two feeds
steps: Run the tests. Three of the five fail. Read the messages: one lists the threads that called ledger.post, and two quote "Emission from another coroutine is detected".
Fix importSettlements by moving one line. Reading and parsing must run on io; posting and the collector must not.
Rewrite bothAcquirers with channelFlow: one launch per feed, and send where the stub calls emit.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them once more.
hints: flowOn moves the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn. Ask which lines must run on io, and put flowOn directly below the last of them.
Inside channelFlow { }, this is a ProducerScope: a CoroutineScope you can launch in and a SendChannel you can send to. You don't need awaitClose; that's for callbackFlow.
You don't need to close the channel or join the children. channelFlow completes by itself when its block and all its children are done.

The test feeds use delay. runTest's virtual clock covers them, because channelFlow's children inherit the test dispatcher. The merged flow should complete at 390 ms of virtual time, the slower feed's last item.

drill.title: Write flowOn by hand from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write myFlowOn(dispatcher) with flow { }, coroutineScope, produce and a for loop over the channel. Then answer without running it: where does the block of flow { } run, where does your emit run, and how many emits can return while the collector holds the first value?

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val mailbox = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { // the upstream runs on dispatcher this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } } for (value in mailbox) emit(value) // our emit runs in the collector's coroutine } } // the upstream's flow { } block runs in the produce coroutine, on dispatcher // 65 emits can return while the collector holds item 1: 64 in the channel, 1 in hand

alt.html: // Java equivalent: an executor for the upstream, a 64-slot queue, a drain loop on the caller static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> mailbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> put(mailbox, value)); put(mailbox, END); }); for (Object v = mailbox.take(); v != END; v = mailbox.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); }

recap: The collector runs inside emit, so emit must run in the collector's context. withContext around emit would drag the collector onto another thread, and flow { } refuses it.
When the dispatcher changes, flowOn runs the upstream in a second coroutine and puts a channel between the two halves, 64 slots by default. The producer can get 65 emits ahead.

flowOn moves only the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn. Two calls make two walls and three rooms; two adjacent calls fuse, and the first one wins. With the same dispatcher, as in flowOn(CoroutineName(...)), there is no channel.
To emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow: send is safe from any child, and the flow completes after every child. produceIn hands you the channel itself, hot, in your scope.
In tests, inject the dispatcher that flowOn uses. flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) inside runTest runs on the real clock.

explain.prompt: A teammate moved a blocking acquirer reader with withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(record) }, got "Flow invariant is violated", and asks why Kotlin forbids something so obvious. Explain it, and say what flowOn does instead.
explain.answer: In a flow, emit isn't a hand-off. It's a direct call into the collector, so the collector's code runs inside emit. If emit ran inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO), our collector, the part that posts to the ledger, would suddenly run on an IO thread it never asked for, maybe with a client that isn't thread-safe. flow { } checks every emit and refuses that. flowOn solves it by breaking the call chain. When the dispatcher changes, it starts a second coroutine on IO that runs everything above flowOn and sends each value into a channel with 64 slots, and on our side a loop takes values out and calls our collector in its own coroutine. So the reader runs on IO, can get up to 65 values ahead, and the collector stays exactly where it was. It only moves what's above it, so we put it right under the blocking read.

deeper.html:
Some details of flowOn only show up in production.

It can lose in-flight values on cancellation. Its KDoc says that "flows operating across different dispatchers might lose some in-flight elements when cancelled", and that the operator "ensures that downstream flow does not resume on cancellation even if the element was already emitted by the upstream flow". For a settlement import that means the reader may have read lines that nobody posted. If that matters, track what was posted, not what was read.

Whether a channel appears depends on dispatcher objects, not threads. With a collector already on Dispatchers.IO, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) stays sequential, with no channel. With a collector on Dispatchers.Default, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) creates one, even though the two dispatchers share threads, because they are different objects.

Stability in 1.11.0: flowOn, channelFlow, callbackFlow and produceIn compile with no opt-in. CoroutineScope.produce, which the hand-built myFlowOn uses, is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. Use the library's operators in real code and keep myFlowOn as the model in your head.

callbackFlow, from lesson 9 of the coroutines track, is a subclass of the same channelFlow builder. The difference is one check: if its block returns while the channel is still open, it throws an IllegalStateException telling you to call awaitClose { ... } at the end. Lesson 8 of this track wraps a listener API with it.

buffer() is the same machine as flowOn without the context change, and neighbouring channel operators fuse into one channel. Lesson 4 of this track takes that apart, using toString() as a peek under the hood.
